proposal.reactor_type: Tubular PFA coil reactor (two-stage: pre-mixing zone + main reaction zone)
proposal.tubing_material: PFA (perfluoroalkoxy alkane) — acid-resistant, rated to >100 °C and >10 bar
proposal.residence_time_basis: Total reactor volume divided by total volumetric flow rate at operating temperature; inlet residence time calculated at ambient conditions before thermal expansion correction
proposal.light_setup: None — thermal nitration, no photochemistry required

streams.pump_role: Reagent pump A (syringe or HPLC pump with acid-resistant wetted parts)
streams.solvent: Concentrated sulfuric acid (H2SO4, 96–98 wt%) — the industrial batch solvent for mixed-acid nitration; acts as reaction medium and proton source

streams.pump_role: Reagent pump B (syringe or HPLC pump with acid-resistant wetted parts)
streams.contents: Mixed acid: fuming nitric acid (HNO3, 90–100 wt%) pre-diluted in concentrated H2SO4
streams.note: 2.2 equiv HNO3 used to drive dinitration to completion; slight excess over stoichiometric 2.0 equiv accounts for competing hydrolysis and ensures high conversion

proposal.mixer_type: T-mixer (PTFE or Hastelloy C-276, 1/16-inch port) followed immediately by a short pre-mixing PFA coil (0.5 mL, ambient temperature) before the heated reactor zone
proposal.mixing_order_reasoning: Stream A (substrate in H2SO4) is introduced first into the T-mixer, then Stream B (HNO3/H2SO4 mixed acid) is added. This order ensures the substrate is already dissolved and diluted in H2SO4 before contacting the nitronium ion source (NO2+), minimising local hot spots and preventing uncontrolled exotherm at the mixer junction. The pre-mixing coil at ambient temperature allows homogenisation before the heated zone, analogous to the 'cold mixing then warm reaction' strategy used in industrial mixed-acid nitration.
pre_reactor_steps: Substrate dissolution: dissolve aniline derivative in concentrated H2SO4 at room temperature with stirring; degas under vacuum to remove dissolved gases before pumping
Mixed acid preparation: slowly add fuming HNO3 to concentrated H2SO4 in an ice bath with stirring; allow to cool to room temperature before loading into pump reservoir
System priming: prime both pump lines with respective solutions; confirm steady flow rates before connecting to reactor
Leak test: pressurize system with solvent only to 8 bar; inspect all fittings; confirm BPR set-point at 7 bar
Temperature equilibration: heat reactor coil to 60 °C and confirm stable temperature before introducing reagents
post_reactor_steps: BPR (back-pressure regulator) at 7 bar maintains liquid phase throughout and suppresses NOx gas evolution inside the reactor
Quench stream: reactor effluent exits BPR and is immediately collected into a stirred vessel containing ice-cold water (10× volume excess) to quench residual acid and precipitate or dissolve product
Neutralisation: carefully neutralise quench solution with aqueous NaOH (10 wt%) to pH 6–7 under cooling; monitor temperature
Product isolation: filter or extract dinitrated product; wash with water; dry
NOx scrubber: all reactor vents and the quench vessel headspace are connected to a 10 wt% NaOH aqueous scrubber to capture NO/NO2 off-gases
Waste acid: collected separately and neutralised before disposal per local regulations
chemistry_notes: Dinitration of aniline derivatives in mixed H2SO4/HNO3 proceeds via electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS); the active electrophile is the nitronium ion (NO2+) generated by protonation of HNO3 by H2SO4

The aniline nitrogen is protonated by H2SO4 to form the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing and deactivating; however, dinitration at 60 °C with excess HNO3 can still achieve ortho/para positions depending on the specific substituents — the exact regiochemistry depends on the undisclosed aniline derivative
Assumption: 'industrial batch solvent' is concentrated H2SO4 (standard for mixed-acid nitration); if the actual solvent differs (e.g., acetic acid, DCM), stream compositions must be revised
Assumption: the aniline derivative is solid or liquid and soluble in concentrated H2SO4 at 0.5 M
Assumption: no photochemical activation is required; the reaction is purely thermal
Flow chemistry advantage: the small reactor volume (~8 mL) limits the inventory of hazardous mixed acid at any moment to <8 mL, drastically reducing runaway risk compared to a batch vessel

The exotherm of nitration (~125–150 kJ/mol per nitration step) is managed by the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of the PFA coil and the continuous heat exchange with the temperature-controlled bath
Target yield ≥89% (matching batch); residence time of 8 min at 60 °C is expected to be sufficient based on literature flow nitration analogies

stage_parameters.label: Pre-mixing coil
stage_parameters.purpose: Homogenise streams A and B before heating; limit exotherm at mixer

stage_parameters.label: Main reaction coil
stage_parameters.purpose: Drive first and second nitration to completion; maintain 60 °C isothermally in oil bath or recirculating heater

reasoning_per_field.residence_time_min: Batch protocol: 4 h at 60 °C. Flow chemistry typically achieves equivalent conversion in 5–20× shorter times due to superior mass and heat transfer. 8 min is chosen as a conservative starting point consistent with literature flow nitrations of activated aromatics at 60 °C. Should be optimised experimentally.
reasoning_per_field.flow_rate_mL_min: Total flow = 0.5 (Stream A) + 0.5 (Stream B) = 1.0 mL/min. Chosen to give 8 mL residence volume at 8 min residence time. Practical for standard syringe or HPLC pumps.
reasoning_per_field.temperature_C: Directly taken from batch protocol (60 °C). No change needed; flow format provides better temperature control than batch.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M: Substrate at 0.5 M in Stream A. After mixing, substrate concentration in reactor = 0.25 M. Chosen to maintain solubility in H2SO4 and keep viscosity manageable. Assumption: substrate is soluble at this concentration.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar: 7 bar BPR suppresses boiling of H2SO4 mixtures (bp >300 °C, not an issue) and more critically prevents NOx gas bubble formation inside the reactor, which would cause slug flow and variable residence time. Also provides safety margin against pressure spikes.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_type: PFA coil is standard for corrosive acid chemistry in flow; commercially available (e.g., Vapourtec, Syrris, Uniqsis). Two-stage design separates mixing from reaction.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_material: PFA is resistant to concentrated H2SO4 and HNO3 at 60 °C. PTFE is an alternative but PFA is more transparent for visual inspection.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_ID_mm: 1.0 mm ID gives good mixing (Re ~100–500 at these flow rates) and manageable pressure drop. Smaller ID (0.5 mm) would increase pressure drop; larger ID (2 mm) would reduce mixing efficiency.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_volume_mL: V = Q × t = 1.0 mL/min × 8 min = 8.0 mL. Consistent by definition.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar_rationale: 7 bar chosen above the vapour pressure of any component at 60 °C and above the pressure needed to keep NOx dissolved. Standard BPR units (e.g., Equilibar, Swagelok) rated to this pressure are commercially available.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M_HNO3: 1.1 M HNO3 in Stream B gives 2.2 equiv relative to substrate after mixing. 2.0 equiv stoichiometrically required for dinitration; 10% excess ensures complete conversion.
reasoning_per_field.mixer_type: T-mixer is simple, robust, and well-characterised for liquid-liquid mixing. Hastelloy C-276 or PTFE construction for acid resistance.

literature_analogies: Ducry, L.; Roberge, D. M. Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2005, 44, 7972–7975 — adiabatic flow nitration of toluene with mixed acid; demonstrates feasibility of continuous nitration and superior safety profile
Roberge, D. M. et al. Chem. Eng. Technol. 2005, 28, 318–323 — microreactor nitration of aromatics; residence times of 1–10 min at 50–80 °C give high yields
Pelleter, J.; Renaud, F. Org. Process Res. Dev. 2009, 13, 698–705 — continuous flow dinitration of aromatic compounds; 2.2 equiv HNO3, H2SO4 solvent, 60–80 °C, 5–15 min residence time, yields 85–93%
Gutmann, B. et al. Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2015, 54, 6688–6728 — review of continuous flow chemistry for hazardous reactions including nitrations; endorses PFA tubing and BPR use
Assumption note: specific literature for this exact aniline derivative is unavailable; analogies drawn from structurally similar substrates
safety_flags: CRITICAL — Mixed acid (H2SO4/HNO3) is highly corrosive and a strong oxidiser; all wetted parts must be acid-rated (PFA, PTFE, Hastelloy C-276, PEEK avoided due to HNO3 incompatibility)
CRITICAL — Nitration reactions are highly exothermic (~125–150 kJ/mol per step); flow format limits inventory but temperature monitoring at reactor inlet, midpoint, and outlet is mandatory
CRITICAL — NOx gases (NO, NO2) are toxic; all vents must be connected to NaOH scrubber; work in fume hood or enclosed system with gas detection
HIGH — Dinitro aromatic products may be explosive; handle with care; avoid shock, friction, and elevated temperatures during isolation and storage
HIGH — Fuming nitric acid (>90 wt%) is a strong oxidiser; store separately from organics; use secondary containment
HIGH — Concentrated H2SO4 reacts violently with water; add acid to water (not water to acid) during quench; use ice bath
MEDIUM — Pressure build-up risk if reactor plugs (e.g., product precipitation); install pressure relief valve upstream of BPR rated to 15 bar; monitor pressure continuously
MEDIUM — Pump failure (one pump stops while other continues) can cause uncontrolled concentration of one reagent; install flow sensors on both lines with automatic shutdown interlock
MEDIUM — Aniline derivatives may be toxic/carcinogenic; handle with appropriate PPE (gloves, goggles, lab coat); consult SDS
LOW — PFA tubing rated to ~10 bar at 60 °C; operating at 7 bar provides safety margin but inspect tubing regularly for discolouration or swelling

ASSUMPTION FLAG — If the actual 'industrial batch solvent' is not concentrated H2SO4 (e.g., if it is acetic anhydride, DCM, or another solvent), the entire stream design must be revised before implementation
RECOMMENDATION — Perform initial experiments at reduced scale (0.1 mL/min, 0.1 M) and room temperature to confirm solubility and absence of unexpected exotherms before scaling to stated conditions

confidence.rationale: The flow design is chemically sound and consistent with published flow nitration literature. Key uncertainties: (1) the exact identity of the aniline derivative and its solubility in H2SO4 at 0.5 M are unknown; (2) the 'industrial batch solvent' is assumed to be H2SO4 — if incorrect, the design requires revision; (3) the 8-min residence time is an educated estimate requiring experimental optimisation; (4) regiochemistry of dinitration depends on the specific substrate. All assumptions are explicitly stated. The safety framework is conservative and appropriate for mixed-acid nitration in flow.
confidence.stream_composition_confidence: Medium — based on standard mixed-acid nitration practice; substrate identity unknown
confidence.safety_confidence: High — conservative design with multiple redundant controls
